general.D009: A phone connection can be mandatory for keeping up with work, family and daily responsibilities. It is the second most common household bill, surpassed only by electricity. In the past year, the average price of wireless telephone services {change} by {pct}%.
general.D011: The price of car insurance isn’t the same for every person. Factors for higher costs can include being a home renter, having less education, being a blue-collar worker, or having a lower credit score, factors that disproportionately affect lower-income individuals.
general.D014: Studies have demonstrated that school meal programs play an important role in overall student health and academic achievement by improving children’s diets and combatting hunger. The National School Lunch Program helps students have free or reduced-price meals.
general.D019: Rents in lower-cost, unsubsidized "workforce housing" sectors have risen sharply, with a recent study showing rents for low-wage Atlantans increasing up to nine times faster than rents for high earners.
general.D021: A lack of reliable transit cuts low-income workers off from the majority of the region's employment opportunities, worsening unemployment and limiting upward mobility.
general.D027: With the rise of fast fashion manufacturing, many clothing items are lower quality and break after fewer wears. Low-income consumers can become trapped in a costly cycle of constantly replacing worn-out clothes.
general.D030: Lacking a full computer restricts workers from building digital skills, running heavy work software, and reliably completing remote employment or educational tasks that require larger screens and physical keyboards. Having more devices means more purchasing and repair costs that can strain families.
general.D033: When cheap or older appliances break down completely, many low-income households cannot afford immediate replacements, forcing them to go without necessities. Older and cheaper appliances can also be less energy efficient, costing people even more in energy bills.
general.D039: Participating in school activities can provide social, emotional, physical and intellectual benefits for children. School activities also strengthen the connections with peers and with their school community, enhancing the likelihood of graduation and preventing dropouts. The costs for these activities can leave students out.
general.D040: Cold weather makes the body work harder, putting stress on the heart to ensure the body stays warm, and exposure to the cold predisposes people to infections like pneumonia. Coats are an essential part of staying safe and healthy during the winter months.
general.D045: Coats are often the most expensive item in a child’s wardrobe, yet they tend to outgrow them quickly. Tight budgets can leave little room for seasonal clothing, yet clothing is not covered by major federal safety nets as food and healthcare are. Not having a coat can lead to school absences, physical health risks, or poor emotional well-being.
general.D048: Missing meals and experiencing chronic hunger significantly impact children's physical growth, cognitive development, and mental health. This becomes a larger issue when school is out of session and it is up to households to find a child’s next meal.
general.D051: Training can give people valuable skills for the workplace. Because they cannot afford the upfront time or money to participate, low-income families can miss out on income boosts from having advanced skills.

cac.D009: Bills can start to add up and cause stress for the money needed to keep a home. In 2025, CAC reported preventing evictions for 1,108 households.
cac.D013: Often, childcare costs do not end at the price for a care program. The CAC offers free coats for kids and school supply bags to help families when the costs start to add up. In 2025, Coats for Kids served 623 children.
cac.D014: Students still need meals even when they are not in school during the summer. In 2025, Meals for Kids served 1,097 children.
cac.D020: Medical bills are a common cause of sudden financial crisis. In 2025, CAC contributed $796,416.64 to prevent homelessness, helping people stay safe and sheltered during times of crisis.
cac.D027: Canopy Thrift has a selective process to choose the items that make it to the floor, helping people gain access to higher quality items. In 2025, clients used $206,768.67 in Canopy Thrift credits.
